utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Madam Registrar, may we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution. MS. DEL PONTE: Good morning, Your Honour. For the Prosecution, Carla Del Ponte; Dan Saxon, trial attorney; Kimberly Fleming, case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the accused, the accused in person, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Under Rule 62, I have to satisfy myself that you are aware that you have the right to counsel. We are aware that you have sent a letter of about 100 pages in handwriting. Unfortunately, it was not possible to translate it until now; therefore, we can't take it today into consideration. But is it still your perspective that you want to defend yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And nothing will change in this respect until the end of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We will see. We are still seized with the motion by the Office of the Prosecutor requesting the assignment of Defence counsel. But as mentioned beforehand, we can't decide before we have heard what your remarks on this issue are. Then following Rule 62(ii), I have to satisfy myself that you have the indictment in a language you understand. And may I ask, are there any problems related to this? During the last appearance, you indicated there would be some problems. But let me tell you this: Based on your intervention, I got into some details of this, as you called it, problem. First of all, all human rights issues have the same language, and telling us that it's a fundamental right of an accused to be informed promptly and in detail in a language which he understands. This is Article 14(3)(a) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights of December 16, 1966. So does the Convent for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms of November 4, 1950, in Article 6(3)(a) which it reads that, The accused has to be informed promptly in the language which he understands. From this it follows that in our Statute it reads in Article 21(4)(a) that the accused has "to be promptly informed and in detail in a language which he understands." You made some objections to the use of some words. For example, the word "opsi" opposed to "opsti"," the word "tocka" opposed to "tacka" and others. I went into some details, and in my conclusion there's not the slightest doubt that this is the language you understand. We have the common roots in the Herzegovinian Serbo-Croatian language, and what we are discussing here are not dialects, not even dialects. These are variants of one and the same language. And the basic document, I am convinced that it's not only in a language you understand but also the language you are using because whenever those words mentioned by you, for example, the word for Defence, which would be in the Croatian variant "obrana" and in the Serb version "odbrana" you can read the Serbian version in the indictment. Therefore, I have to ask you: Are there any other objections to my understanding that you have the indictment as such before you in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is correct, Your Honour. I have received the indictment in the Serbian language. However, it was not read out in its entirety in the Serbian language. There were many expressions I do not understand. Like you in the meantime, I consulted some linguistic experts about some words which I absolutely do not understand. These experts explained to me that the noun "tocka" could be the feminine variant of the word "tacka" and as for the word "Hotimicno," and I still insist I do not understand it, they explained that there is an Albanian tribe called Hoti, and Micno would be derived from Mitici, which means "to move," so it would mean Hoti moving or someone moving in the way the Hoti move. These are big problems, and I insist that you find an interpreter who can speak the Serbian language well. I cannot speculate. The word "Hotimicno," is an artificial word, and it sounds in Serbian just Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. as cockney might sound in London in relation to standard English. It is my right to have the interpreter interpret to me in the Serbian standard language and not to use some sort of jargon or an artificial language, a language used in Zagreb and elsewhere. I have received the indictment in the Serbian language, and I can plead today to all counts of the indictment, but there is another very important problem. Let me remind you that Article 20 of the Statute under 3 says "The Trial Chamber shall read the indictment," shall "convince itself that the rights of the accused are respected," and shall ask the accused to plead. Your Honour, with all due respect, because I see that you are acting properly, I do not see the Chamber here. It says in Rule 62, The accused shall without delay be brought before the Trial Chamber or a permanent Judge thereof without delay and shall be formally charged. "The Trial Chamber" or the Judge shall, "read or have the indictment read out to the accused in a language the accused speaks and understands, and satisfy itself," himself, or herself, "that the accused understands the indictment." However, if the Rules of Procedure and Evidence are not in accordance with the Statute, it is the Statute that has precedence because the Statute was brought by those who founded the Tribunal, while the Rules of Procedure and Evidence were brought by the Tribunal itself. This may seem to be a formal issue to you, but I feel that it is essential. I feel that the entire Chamber should be present when I am pleading because I feel that this is a very important part of the trial, maybe the most important. I wish to look all the members of the Trial Chamber in the eye. I want them all to see what my bearing is and whether I am convincing or not when I plead not guilty. And also it says here that it is the Trial Chamber that should read out the indictment and not just any clerk of the Court. Therefore, I demand that the indictment be read out again, that it be read out by the Trial Chamber. You don't all have to read it -- you don't have to read all of it yourself. The Judges might take turns reading it. And I feel that all the provisions of the Statute, first, and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, secondly, should be respected. If there is any conflict between the Statute and the Rules, it is the Statute that should be strictly respected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj, I appreciate that you admit that you have the indictment before you in a language you understand. As regards the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, there is a huge discussion given to the Judges implementing the Statute and under the Statute it clearly reads that a Pre-Trial Judge has to do this Initial Appearance. And you have followed the decisions from the President assigning the case to the Trial Chamber and then assigning the case to me. So there is no procedural problem. I'm here sitting as a representative of Trial Chamber II, and then we may proceed immediately under Rule 62. You are informed, and I have satisfied myself that you have the indictment in a language you understand. So therefore, may I ask Madam Registrar to read from the indictment count by count the charges.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 1: Prosecutions on political, racial, or religious grounds, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(h) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I hare your plea.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty. Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 2, extermination, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(b) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 3, murder, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(a) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 4, murder, a violation of the laws or customs of war as recognised by common Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 punishable under Articles 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 5, imprisonment, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(e) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 6, torture, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(f) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never in my life have I ever tortured anyone, and I am not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 7, inhuman acts, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(i) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 8, torture, a violation of the laws or customs of war as recognised by Common Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 punishable under Articles 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 9, cruel treatment, a violation of the laws or customs of war as recognised by Common Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Articles 3, and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 10, deportation, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(d) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 11, inhuman acts, forcible transfers, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(i) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 12, wanton destruction of villages or devastation not justified by military necessity, a violence of the laws or customs of war, punishable under Articles 3(b) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 13, destruction or wilful damage done to institutions dedicated to religion or education, a violation of the laws or customs of war, punishable under Articles 3(b) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again you are mentioning these Albanian Hoti, the Albanian tribe of Hoti, but I'm not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 14, plunder of public or private property, a violation of the laws or customs of war, punishable under Articles 3(e) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One moment, please. Madam Registrar, we can conclude that the accused has pleaded not guilty to all the counts of the indictment we have before us. This concludes the first part of the further appearance. And let's turn now to the Status Conference in order to discuss the remaining administrative issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: adjourned at 9.54 a.m., to be followed by a Status Conference 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
